source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 9 (PDF 192-228, printed 189-225); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 9 (Electrostatics and Current Electricity), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 State Coulomb's law. Write it in vector form and show that the Coulomb forces between two charges are equal and opposite. How is the force changed when the charges are placed in a dielectric medium? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statement: The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them:
F ∝ q₁q₂/r², or F = k q₁q₂/r² ... (9.1)
The force acts along the line joining the two charges. k depends on the medium and the system of units. For free space in SI units:
k = 1/4πε₀ ... (9.2), where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² (permittivity of free space), so k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
F = (1/4πε₀)(q₁q₂/r²) ... (9.3)

Vector form: Let r̂₂₁ be the unit vector from q₁ to q₂ and r̂₁₂ the unit vector from q₂ to q₁ (Fig. 9.2).
F₂₁ = (1/4πε₀)(q₁q₂/r²) r̂₂₁ ... (9.5) (force on q₂ due to q₁)
F₁₂ = (1/4πε₀)(q₁q₂/r²) r̂₁₂ ... (9.6) (force on q₁ due to q₂)
Since r̂₂₁ = −r̂₁₂, F₂₁ = −F₁₂: the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (Coulomb's force is mutual). The signs of the charges decide whether the forces are attractive or repulsive.

Effect of medium: An insulating medium is called a dielectric. A dielectric always reduces the force compared with free space by a constant factor, the relative permittivity εᵣ (Table 9.1). In a medium:
F = (1/4πε₀εᵣ)(q₁q₂/r²), i.e. εᵣ times smaller than in free space.
For air εᵣ = 1.0006, so Eq. 9.3 gives the force in air with negligible error.

book_ref.quote: To represent the direction of these forces, we introduce unit vectors.

blocks.prompt: 2 A charge q₁ = −20 μC is at the corner of a right angle. A charge q₂ = +40 μC is 0.20 m from q₁ along the x-axis and a charge q₃ = +30 μC is 0.30 m from q₁ along the y-axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the net force on q₁. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both forces on q₁ are attractive and at right angles; find each by Coulomb's law, then combine them like rectangular components.

book_ref.quote: To find the resultant of F₁₂ and F₁₃, let us make free-body diagram

steps: tan θ = F₁₃/F₁₂ = 60/180 = 0.333, θ = 18.4° with the line joining q₁ and q₂
blocks.final_answer: Net force on q₁ = 190 N at 18.4° to the line q₁q₂ (towards the side of q₃)

blocks.prompt: 3 Define electric intensity and give its unit. What are electric field lines? Describe the field-line patterns of an isolated positive charge, two identical positive charges, two equal and opposite charges and parallel charged plates, and list the properties of field lines. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electric intensity: the force experienced by a unit positive charge placed at a point: E = F/q ... (9.8). It is a vector in the direction of F; unit N C⁻¹. Also F = qE ... (9.9).

Field lines: proposed by Michael Faraday, they are a visual map of the direction and strength of the field around a charged object (also called electric lines of force). The number of lines per unit area passing perpendicularly through a surface is proportional to the magnitude of E.

Patterns:
(1) Isolated +q: a positive test charge is repelled, so lines are directed radially outward (Fig. 9.5); for −q they are radially inward (Fig. 9.6). Lines are closer near the charge (strong field) and spread out farther away.
(2) Two identical positive charges: the lines are curved and seem to repel each other; the middle region has a zero field spot or neutral zone (Fig. 9.7).
(3) Equal and opposite charges: lines start on the positive charge and end on the negative charge; the field at any point is the resultant of both, along the tangent (Fig. 9.8).
(4) Parallel plates: in the middle region the lines are parallel and equally spaced, so the field is uniform (Fig. 9.9).

Properties:
• Lines originate from positive charges and end on negative charges.
• The tangent to a line at any point gives the direction of E there.
• Lines are closer where the field is strong and farther apart where it is weak.
• No two lines cross each other, because E has only one direction at any point.

book_ref.quote: We are now in a position to summarize the properties of electric field lines.

blocks.prompt: 4 Two positive point charges of 25 μC and 4 μC are 2.8 m apart. Find the point on the line joining them where the electric field is zero, and the field that each charge produces there. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Between two like charges the two fields are opposite; the zero point is where their magnitudes are equal, nearer the smaller charge.

book_ref.quote: Find the spot on the line joining the two charges where electric field is zero.

steps: Let P be at distance d from the 4 μC charge. At P: E₁ = E₂, so k(25 μC)/(2.8 − d)² = k(4 μC)/d²
Taking square roots: 5/(2.8 − d) = 2/d, so 5d = 5.6 − 2d, 7d = 5.6, d = 0.8 m
(The other root lies outside the charges, where the two fields point the same way and cannot cancel.)
blocks.final_answer: E = 0 at 0.8 m from the 4 μC charge (2.0 m from the 25 μC charge); each field there is 5.6 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹, in opposite directions

blocks.prompt: 5 Define electric flux and write it as a scalar product. Explain the flux when the area is perpendicular, parallel and inclined to the field. Show that the total flux through a sphere with a point charge q at its centre is q/ε₀. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electric flux: the number of field lines passing through a given element of area, φₑ. The area is represented by a vector area A, of magnitude A and direction along the normal to the area.

(a) Area perpendicular to the lines: EA lines pass through it, φₑ = EA (maximum).
(b) Area parallel to the lines: no line crosses it; E and A are perpendicular, φₑ = EA cos 90° = 0.
(c) Area inclined, its normal at angle θ to E: the projection perpendicular to the lines is A cos θ, so φₑ = EA cos θ.
In general φₑ = EA cos θ = E·A ... (9.10). Flux is a scalar; SI unit N m² C⁻¹.

Flux through a sphere: Let charge q be at the centre of a sphere of radius r (Fig. 9.12). Divide the surface into n small flat patches ΔA₁, ΔA₂, …, ΔAₙ (vector areas outward). Total flux:
φₑ = E₁·ΔA₁ + E₂·ΔA₂ + … + Eₙ·ΔAₙ ... (9.11)
At each patch E is along ΔA (θ = 0°, cos 0° = 1) and has the same magnitude:
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²) ... (9.12)
φₑ = E(ΔA₁ + ΔA₂ + … + ΔAₙ) = E × (total area 4πr²)
φₑ = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²) × 4πr²
φₑ = q/ε₀ ... (9.13)

Any closed surface S enclosing the sphere has the same flux (Fig. 9.13), so the total flux does not depend on the shape of the closed surface; it depends on the medium and the charge enclosed.

book_ref.quote: Let us calculate the electric flux through a closed surface, in shape of a sphere of radius r

blocks.prompt: 6 A flat sheet of area 0.25 m² is in a uniform field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Find the flux through it when (i) its normal makes 30° with the field (ii) the sheet is parallel to the field. (iii) Find also the total flux through a closed surface enclosing a charge of 5 μC. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use φₑ = EA cos θ with θ the angle between E and the normal; for a closed surface only the enclosed charge matters.

book_ref.quote: Figure 9.11(c) shows the case when A is neither perpendicular nor parallel to field lines

steps: (ii) Sheet parallel to E: its normal is at 90° to E, φₑ = EA cos 90° = 0
blocks.final_answer: (i) 4.33 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹ (ii) zero (iii) 5.65 × 10⁵ N m² C⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 7 State Gauss's law and derive it for a number of point charges inside a closed surface. Use it to find the electric field at a point outside a charged conducting sphere. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Derivation: Let point charges q₁, q₂, …, qₙ be distributed inside an arbitrary closed surface (Fig. 9.14). The flux due to each charge through the closed surface is q/ε₀, whatever the shape, so:
φₑ = q₁/ε₀ + q₂/ε₀ + … + qₙ/ε₀
φₑ = (1/ε₀)(q₁ + q₂ + … + qₙ)
φₑ = Q/ε₀ ... (9.14), where Q is the total charge enclosed.
Gauss's law: The total electric flux through any closed surface is 1/ε₀ times the total charge enclosed in it.

Gaussian surface: an imaginary closed surface through the point where E is required, chosen so that the flux through it is easily found.

Field of a charged conducting sphere: A conducting sphere of radius R has charge q spread uniformly over its surface (Fig. 9.15). By spherical symmetry E is radial and has the same magnitude at every point of a concentric sphere. Take a Gaussian sphere of radius r > R.
Flux: φₑ = EA = E × 4πr²
Gauss's law: φₑ = q/ε₀
So E × 4πr² = q/ε₀
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²)
The field outside is the same as though the whole charge were concentrated at the centre. Just outside the surface (r = R):
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/R²) ... (9.15); in vector form E = (1/4πε₀)(q/R²) r̂.

book_ref.quote: The area of the Gaussian sphere is 4πr², and because E is uniform over the sphere

blocks.prompt: 8 A conducting sphere of radius 0.15 m carries a charge of 3 μC. Find (i) the electric field just outside its surface (ii) the field at 0.45 m from its centre (iii) the total flux through a Gaussian sphere of radius 0.45 m. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Outside, treat the whole charge as if at the centre; the flux depends only on the charge enclosed, not on the radius.

book_ref.quote: Consider a conducting sphere of radius R containing a charge q.

blocks.final_answer: (i) 1.2 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹ (ii) 1.3 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹ (iii) 3.4 × 10⁵ N m² C⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 9 Define electric potential energy difference and potential difference between two points in a uniform field, and the volt. Derive the relation between electric intensity and potential difference between two parallel plates, and show that V m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Potential energy difference: Two oppositely charged parallel plates give a uniform field E (Fig. 9.16). A positive charge q is carried from A to B against the field in equilibrium (uniform velocity) by a force F equal and opposite to qE. The work done W_AB increases its electrical P.E.:
ΔU = U_B − U_A = W_AB ... (9.16)

Potential difference: the work done in carrying a unit positive charge from A to B in equilibrium:
ΔV = V_B − V_A = W_AB/q = ΔU/q ... (9.17), so ΔU = qΔV ... (9.18)
Unit: 1 volt = 1 joule/1 coulomb ... (9.19); 1 V exists between two points if 1 J of work is done in moving 1 C between them. Potential and potential difference are scalars.

Relation with E: V_B − V_A = W_AB/q ... (9.21)
Here W_AB = Fd = −qEd (F must be opposite to qE to keep the charge in equilibrium).
V_B − V_A = −qEd/q = −Ed
E = −(V_B − V_A)/d = −ΔV/d ... (9.22)
For an infinitesimally small separation Δd:
E = −ΔV/Δd ... (9.23)
ΔV/Δd is the potential gradient (the maximum rate of change of potential with distance, along a field line). So E equals the negative of the potential gradient; the negative sign shows that E points towards decreasing potential.

Unit: 1 V m⁻¹ = 1 (J C⁻¹)/m = 1 (N m)/(m C) = 1 N C⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: In this section, we will establish a relation between electric intensity and potential difference.

blocks.prompt: 10 Two parallel plates 4 mm apart are connected to a 600 V supply. Find (i) the electric intensity between them (ii) the force on an electron between the plates (iii) the work done in carrying a proton from the negative to the positive plate. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The field is uniform, so E = ΔV/Δd; the force is F = qE and the work is W = qΔV.

book_ref.quote: These are connected to a battery of 12 volts. Find the magnitude of electric field intensity between them.

steps: (ii) F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.5 × 10⁵ = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N (towards the positive plate)

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the motion of an electron released from rest at the negative plate of two charged parallel plates: find its acceleration and the speed with which it reaches the positive plate. What is its path if it enters perpendicular to the field? Define the electron volt. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Field and force: Two oppositely charged parallel plates produce a uniform field from the positive to the negative plate. With potential difference V and separation d:
E = V/d ... (9.27)
The force on a charge q is F = qE ... (9.26). A positive charge moves along E; a negative charge (electron) moves opposite to E, towards the positive plate.

Acceleration: By F = ma,
a = F/m = qE/m
For an electron q = e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

Final speed: Released from rest (vi = 0) at the negative plate, it covers S = d. By the third equation of motion:
2aS = vf² − vi², so v² = 2ad and v = √(2ad)
(Equivalently, loss of P.E. = gain in K.E.: eV = ½mv².)
Example from the text: V = 20 V, d = 2 × 10⁻² m gives E = 1000 N C⁻¹, a = 1.76 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻², v² = 7.04 × 10¹² m² s⁻², v = 2.65 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

Path across the field: If the charged particle enters perpendicular to the uniform field, its horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical velocity is accelerated by the electric force, so its path is parabolic, like a projectile thrown horizontally. A positive particle bends towards the negative plate; a negative one towards the positive plate. Moving along a uniform field, the path is straight.

Electron volt: the energy acquired or lost by an electron as it traverses a potential difference of one volt. ΔK.E. = eΔV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1 V), so
1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ... (9.25)

book_ref.quote: To understand the effect of uniform electric field on the motion of charged particles

blocks.prompt: 12 Two parallel plates 1.5 cm apart have a potential difference of 45 V. An electron is released from rest at the negative plate. Find (i) the field between the plates (ii) the acceleration of the electron (iii) its speed on reaching the positive plate and its kinetic energy in eV. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find E = V/d, then a = eE/m, then the third equation of motion with vi = 0 and S = d.

book_ref.quote: If the electron is released from the negative plate, the velocity gained by it when it reaches positive plate

blocks.final_answer: (i) 3000 N C⁻¹ (ii) 5.27 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻² (iii) 3.98 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹; K.E. = 45 eV

blocks.prompt: 13 What is meant by drift velocity? Why is a current set up almost instantly although the drift velocity is small? Derive the relation I = nAvq for the current through a conductor. What is conventional current? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Drift velocity: When a conductor is connected to a battery, an electric field is set up inside it and the free electrons experience a force along −E. They keep colliding with the atoms, transferring energy to the lattice, so they are not accelerated in a straight line; they acquire an average velocity along −E, the drift velocity (very small, of the order of 10⁻³ m s⁻¹ or less). This drift forms the current.

Instant current: On switching ON, all free electrons in the circuit start drifting at once; they repel neighbouring ones and the disturbance propagates almost instantaneously, so a bulb lights at once.

Current: I = Q/t ... (9.28); unit ampere (1 C s⁻¹).

Derivation of I = nAvq: Take a segment of length L and cross-section A (volume AL) (Fig. 9.21). With n charge carriers per unit volume, the number in the segment is nAL; with charge q on each:
Q = nALq ... (9.29)
If the drift velocity is v, the time for all these carriers to leave through one face is
t = L/v
By definition I = Q/t:
I = nALq/(L/v)
I = nAvq ... (9.30)

Conventional current: the hypothetical flow of positive charges that would have the same effect as the actual flow of negative charges. It flows from higher to lower potential (from the positive towards the negative terminal outside the source); I always means conventional current.

book_ref.quote: Suppose that charge carriers move towards left face of the segment

blocks.prompt: 14 A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a current of 4.5 A. Find (i) the drift velocity of the electrons (ii) the charge passing through the wire in 2 minutes (iii) the number of electrons passing in that time. (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rearrange I = nAvq for v; then Q = It and N = Q/e.

book_ref.quote: calculate the drift velocity of the electrons in the wire

blocks.prompt: 15 State Ohm's law. Define resistivity and conductivity with their units. Explain why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature, define the temperature coefficient of resistance and derive α in terms of resistivity. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ohm's law: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided there is no change in its physical state: V ∝ I, V = RI ... (9.31). 1 Ω: 1 A flows when 1 V is applied.

Resistivity: R ∝ L/A, so R = ρL/A ... (9.32), and ρ = RA/L ... (9.33). Resistivity (specific resistance) is the resistance of a metre cube of the material; unit Ω m. Resistance is a characteristic of a particular wire; resistivity is a property of the material.
Conductance G = 1/R; conductivity σ = 1/ρ ... (9.34), unit Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ (mho m⁻¹).

Effect of temperature: Resistance is due to collisions of free electrons with lattice atoms. As temperature rises, the amplitude of vibration of the atoms increases, their collision cross-section grows, collisions become more frequent and the resistance increases.

Temperature coefficient: The change in resistance is nearly linear over a wide range (Fig. 9.22). The fractional change in resistance per kelvin is
α = (Rt − Ro)/(Ro t) ... (9.35)
where Ro and Rt are the resistances at 0 °C and t °C. Since
Rt = ρt L/A and Ro = ρo L/A ... (9.36)
substituting in Eq. 9.35 (L/A cancels):
α = (ρt − ρo)/(ρo t) ... (9.37)
Unit K⁻¹. Germanium, silicon, etc. have negative α (resistance falls as temperature rises).

book_ref.quote: The resistivity of a substance depends upon the temperature also.

blocks.prompt: 16 A copper wire is 20 m long and has a cross-sectional area of 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m². Taking the resistivity of copper 1.69 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m as its value at 0 °C and α = 0.0039 K⁻¹, find (i) its resistance at 0 °C (ii) its resistance at 80 °C. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use R = ρL/A for Ro, then rearrange α = (Rt − Ro)/(Ro t) as Rt = Ro(1 + αt).

book_ref.quote: Compute the resistivity of iron.

blocks.prompt: 17 What is electrical power? Derive P = VI for the power supplied by a battery to a resistor, and obtain the other two forms of the power dissipated in a resistor. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a battery of emf ε in series with a resistance R (Fig. 9.23). A steady current I flows and a steady p.d. V exists across R; terminal A (joined to the positive pole) is at higher potential than B. The battery continuously lifts charge uphill through V.

Work done in moving charge Q through p.d. V (the energy supplied by the battery):
W = V × Q ... (9.38)

Electrical power is the rate at which the battery supplies electrical energy:
Power = Energy supplied/Time taken = V(Q/t)
Since I = Q/t:
Electrical power = V × I ... (9.39)
This is a general relation for power delivered by a source of current I at voltage V. By conservation of energy, the power dissipated in R is also P = VI.

Other forms: put V = IR: P = IR × I = I²R; put I = V/R: P = V × V/R = V²/R.
So P = VI, P = I²R, P = V²/R ... (9.40)
With V in volts and I in amperes, P is in watts.

book_ref.quote: Consider a circuit consisting of a battery of emf ε connected in series with a resistance R

blocks.prompt: 18 An electric heater is rated 1000 W, 220 V. Find (i) the current it draws (ii) its resistance (iii) the energy it uses in 30 minutes (iv) its power if it is run on 110 V, assuming its resistance does not change. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use P = VI for the current, P = V²/R for the resistance, energy = P × t, and P = V²/R again at the new voltage.

book_ref.quote: Equation 9.39 is a general relation for power delivered from a source of current I

steps: (iv) P = V²/R = 110²/48.4 = 250 W (half the voltage gives one-fourth the power)

blocks.prompt: 19 Define emf and internal resistance. For a cell of emf E and internal resistance r connected to an external resistance R, derive E = IR + Ir and interpret it in terms of energy. Distinguish the emf from the terminal potential difference. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Emf: A cell maintains a steady current; a charge Q passing through it enters at the low potential end and leaves at the high potential end, so the cell must supply energy W. Emf is the energy supplied to unit charge by the cell:
E = W/Q ... (9.41)
It is not a force; unit J C⁻¹ = volt. The energy comes from chemical energy converted inside the cell.

Internal resistance: the resistance of the cell itself, due to the electrolyte between its electrodes. A cell is equivalent to a pure emf E in series with r (Fig. 9.25).

Derivation: With external resistance R (Fig. 9.26), the total resistance is R + r, so
I = E/(R + r)
E = IR + Ir ... (9.42)
IR = V is the terminal potential difference with current I. With the switch open (no current) the voltmeter reads E; with current, V = E − Ir, less than E by Ir.

Energy interpretation: E is the energy gained by unit charge passing through the cell from − to +. Of this, Ir is dissipated inside the cell and IR is dissipated in the external resistance. The potential drops account for the dissipation of the energy supplied by the cell.

Emf vs p.d.: the emf is the cause and the potential difference is its effect; the emf is present even when no current is drawn, but the p.d. across a conductor is zero when no current flows through it.

book_ref.quote: Let us consider the performance of a cell of emf E and internal resistance r

blocks.prompt: 20 A battery reads 9.0 V on open circuit. When a 4.0 Ω resistor is connected across it, the terminal potential difference falls to 8.0 V. Find (i) the current (ii) the internal resistance (iii) the power wasted inside the battery and the total power supplied by it. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The open-circuit reading is the emf; use V = IR for I, then E = V + Ir for r, and I²r and EI for the powers.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the current and the internal resistance of the battery.

steps: (iii) Power wasted inside = I²r = 2.0² × 0.5 = 2.0 W; power in R = VI = 8.0 × 2.0 = 16 W
Total power supplied = EI = 9.0 × 2.0 = 18 W (= 16 W + 2 W)
blocks.final_answer: (i) 2.0 A (ii) 0.5 Ω (iii) 2.0 W wasted inside; 18 W supplied in total

blocks.prompt: 21 Show that Kirchhoff's first rule follows from conservation of charge and derive Kirchhoff's second rule from conservation of energy for a loop containing two cells and two resistors. Give the sign rules for potential changes and the steps for solving a network with loop currents. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
First rule: The sum of all currents meeting at a point is zero, ΣI = 0 ... (9.43) (currents towards the point positive, away negative). For four wires at A (Fig. 9.27), with I₁, I₂ in and I₃, I₄ out:
I₁ + I₂ + (−I₃) + (−I₄) = 0, or I₁ + I₂ = I₃ + I₄ ... (9.44)
i.e. the sum of currents towards a point equals the sum away from it. If there is no source or sink of charge at the point, the charge flowing in must equal the charge flowing out: conservation of charge.

Second rule: In the closed circuit of Fig. 9.28 let E₁ > E₂, so the current I flows counter-clockwise. A charge Q:
• passing through E₁ from − to + gains energy E₁Q;
• passing through E₂ from + to − loses energy −E₂Q;
• passing through R₁ and R₂ (high to low potential) loses −IR₁Q and −IR₂Q.
Returning to its starting point, the total change in its energy is zero (conservation of energy):
E₁Q − IR₁Q − E₂Q − IR₂Q = 0
E₁ − IR₁ − E₂ − IR₂ = 0 ... (9.45)
Kirchhoff's second rule: the algebraic sum of potential changes in a closed circuit is zero.

Sign rules (as corrected): cell crossed from − to +: +E; from + to −: −E. Resistor crossed in the direction of current: −IR; against the current: +IR.

Procedure: (1) Draw the circuit. (2) Choose loops so that each resistance is included at least once. (3) Assume a loop current in each loop, all in the same sense (clockwise or anticlockwise). (4) Write the loop equations (low to high potential positive, high to low negative); in a shared resistor the current is the difference of the loop currents. (5) Solve for the unknowns.

book_ref.quote: According to the law of conservation of energy, the total change in energy of our system is zero.

blocks.prompt: 22 In a single closed loop like Fig. 9.28, a cell of emf E₁ = 15 V and a cell of emf E₂ = 6 V oppose each other, with R₁ = 2 Ω and R₂ = 4 Ω in series (internal resistances negligible). Find (i) the current (ii) the potential difference across each resistor (iii) check that the power given by E₁ equals the power used in the rest of the loop. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Apply E₁ − IR₁ − E₂ − IR₂ = 0; the larger emf decides the direction of the current.

book_ref.quote: Consider a closed circuit shown in Fig. 9.28.

steps: (i) 15 − 2I − 6 − 4I = 0, so 6I = 9 and I = 1.5 A (in the direction driven by E₁)
(iii) Power given by E₁ = E₁I = 15 × 1.5 = 22.5 W
Power used: I²R₁ + I²R₂ + E₂I = 4.5 + 9 + 9 = 22.5 W (energy is conserved)
blocks.final_answer: (i) 1.5 A (ii) 3 V across R₁, 6 V across R₂ (iii) 22.5 W supplied = 22.5 W used

blocks.prompt: 23 Describe the Wheatstone bridge circuit. Derive the condition for no current through the galvanometer, and explain how the bridge is used with the null method to find an unknown resistance. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Circuit: Four resistances R₁, R₂, R₃ and R₄ form a mesh ABCDA (Fig. 9.30). A battery is connected between A and C and a sensitive galvanometer (resistance R_g) between B and D. With the switch closed a current generally flows through the galvanometer; we find the condition for no current.

Balance condition (as corrected): When no current flows through the galvanometer, one current I flows through R₁ and R₂ (path ABC) and another current I′ through R₃ and R₄ (path ADC). No current through the galvanometer means B and D are at the same potential. Hence the potential drop from A to B equals that from A to D, and the drop from B to C equals that from D to C:
IR₁ = I′R₃
IR₂ = I′R₄
Dividing the first equation by the second:
R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄ ... (9.51)
Whenever Eq. 9.51 holds the galvanometer shows no deflection, and conversely.

Finding an unknown resistance (null method): R₁, R₂, R₃ are known adjustable resistances and R₄ is unknown. They are adjusted until the galvanometer shows no deflection; then
R₄ = R₂R₃/R₁
At null no current passes through the galvanometer, so its own resistance does not affect the result, and a sensitive galvanometer (about 10⁻⁶ A) makes the balance point clear.

blocks.prompt: 24 A Wheatstone bridge is balanced with R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 250 Ω and R₃ = 40 Ω. (i) Find the unknown resistance R₄. (ii) R₄ is a wire 2.0 m long with cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m²; find the resistivity of its material. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: At balance R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄; then use ρ = RA/L for the wire.

book_ref.quote: Thus, whenever the condition of Eq. 9.51 is satisfied, no current flows through the galvanometer

steps: (i) R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄, so R₄ = R₂R₃/R₁ = 250 × 40/100 = 100 Ω

blocks.prompt: 25 Why can an ordinary voltmeter not measure the emf of a cell exactly? Explain the potential divider, and derive the expressions used with a potentiometer to measure an unknown emf and to compare the emfs of two cells. Why is the method accurate? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Voltmeter limitation: A voltmeter reads correctly only if it draws no current; unless its resistance is very large it alters the circuit current and the p.d. An ideal voltmeter would need infinite resistance. Digital voltmeters and CROs draw almost no current but are expensive; a potentiometer is simple and accurate.

Potential divider: A resistor R in the form of a wire AB has a sliding contact C (Fig. 9.31). A battery of emf E across R sends I = E/R. If the resistance between A and C is r, the drop between A and C is rI = rE/R; as C moves from A to B, it varies from 0 to E.

Measuring an unknown emf (Fig. 9.32): R is a straight uniform wire. The cell Eₓ is connected between A and the slider C through a galvanometer, with the positive terminals of Eₓ and of the divider both at A. C is adjusted until the galvanometer shows no deflection; then Eₓ equals the p.d. between A and C. For a uniform wire, resistance ∝ length, so
Eₓ = E r/R = E l/L ... (9.52)
where L is the length of AB and l the balancing length AC. Eₓ must not exceed E, otherwise no null point is found.

Comparing two emfs: Find balancing lengths l₁ and l₂ for the two cells:
E₁ = E l₁/L and E₂ = E l₂/L
Dividing: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ ... (9.53)

Principle and accuracy: With a steady current, the potential drop along a uniform wire is proportional to its length (V ∝ l). The emf is measured at the null point, when no current is drawn from the cell, so the potentiometer is one of the most accurate methods of measuring potential.

book_ref.quote: Such an arrangement also known as potential divider can be used to measure the unknown emf

blocks.prompt: 26 A driver cell of emf 2.0 V is connected across a uniform potentiometer wire 100 cm long. (i) At what length will a cell of emf 1.5 V balance? (ii) Another cell balances at 54 cm; find its emf. (iii) Find the ratio of the emfs of the two cells. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The drop along the wire is proportional to length: Eₓ = E l/L, and the ratio of emfs equals the ratio of balancing lengths.

book_ref.quote: The balancing lengths l₁ and l₂ are found separately for the two cells.

steps: (i) Eₓ = E l/L, so l = Eₓ L/E = 1.5 × 100/2.0 = 75 cm

blocks.prompt: 27 What are thermistors and light dependent resistors? Explain why their resistance changes with temperature and light respectively, how they are made, and how each is used in a voltage divider to work a switch or an alarm. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Thermistor: a heat sensitive resistor. Most have a negative temperature coefficient: resistance decreases as temperature increases, because more energy lets the charge carriers (electrons or holes) move more freely (positive-coefficient types also exist). Made by heating, under high pressure, semiconductor ceramic of metallic oxides (manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper, iron), pressed into beads, rods or washers and baked.
Uses: temperature measurement and sensing (thermometers, car coolant sensors; accurate near 10 K), temperature compensation, inrush current limiting.
Voltage divider / fire alarm (Fig. 9.35, as corrected): the thermistor is between B and earth. When heated its resistance falls, so the voltage across it (the potential at B) decreases; the NOT gate input goes low, its output goes high and the siren turns ON.

LDR (photo resistor): a resistor whose resistance decreases with increasing light intensity; made of a semiconductor such as cadmium sulphide deposited in a pattern on an insulating plate.
Principle: in darkness the material has few free electrons, so its resistance is high; light photons give energy to outer electrons and free them, so conductivity increases and resistance falls.
Voltage divider (Fig. 9.36): the LDR is in series with a standard 100 kΩ resistor. In the dark its resistance is much larger, so most of the voltage drops across it (high voltmeter reading); in light its resistance becomes very low and the reading falls. Joining mid-point B to an NPN transistor or a NOT gate makes the LDR a light-operated switch (street lights ON at dusk, OFF at dawn). LDRs also set camera exposure time.

blocks.prompt: 28 An LDR is connected in series with a 100 kΩ resistor across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Find the current and the voltage across the LDR when its resistance is (i) 1.0 MΩ in the dark (ii) 1.0 kΩ in bright light. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The same current flows through both resistors: I = E/(total resistance), then V = IR across the LDR.

book_ref.quote: Hence, the change in light intensity gives rise to change in voltage.

blocks.final_answer: (i) 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ A, 5.5 V across the LDR (ii) 5.9 × 10⁻⁵ A, 0.059 V across the LDR: light makes the voltage fall sharply
